ideas.risks: If the intended theorem is minimax over a class of processes rather than literal per-process learnability, the sparse-spike counterexample may only expose a quantifier mismatch.
ideas.summary: Verify the solver's sparse vanishing-spike refutation line by line: beta(h)=1 via action a=0 at spike times, the best fixed comparator has expected payoff at most 1 for every horizon, and the continuum maximum exists. Then try to strengthen it to a family with beta=1 and regret bounded by any prescribed sublinear envelope.
ideas.title: Audit the Refutation
ideas.why_promising: This is the shortest path to a rigorous conclusion about the stated iff: the unweighted tail condition appears to count long delays at actions with negligible payoff.

ideas.risks: The essential supremum over histories may still be too strong; rare histories or isolated times can violate gamma without causing linear expected regret.
ideas.summary: Replace beta by the payoff-weighted tail gamma(h)=sup_t sup_a esssup a Pr(h<tau_t(a)<infty | history). Prove the same upper bound with T gamma(H) in place of T beta(H), and show equivalence to uniform tightness over positive-scale actions a>=epsilon for every epsilon>0. Then test whether gamma(h)->0 is necessary or only sufficient.
ideas.title: Payoff-Weighted Tail
ideas.why_promising: It directly repairs the solver's obstruction: long delays at a=0 or tiny quote levels should not matter for regret.

ideas.risks: Necessity may fail because an algorithm can exploit predictable price structure rather than waiting for delayed reward feedback.
ideas.summary: Study the ex-ante horizon-level truncation error Delta_T(H)=sup_a sum_{t<=T} E[a 1{H<tau_t(a)<=T-t}]. Establish sufficiency when some H_T has H_T log T=o(T) and Delta_T(H_T)=o(T), using the same delayed-grid reduction. Investigate whether this is closer to a true characterization than uniform gamma.
ideas.title: Horizon Tail Error
ideas.why_promising: This is the weakest condition visible from the truncation proof and avoids beta's worst-case sup over irrelevant times and histories.

ideas.risks: Failure of beta alone is too weak for lower bounds; any theorem will likely need positive payoff scale, positive density in time, and unpredictability assumptions.
ideas.summary: If the intended statement is uniform over a class of processes, formulate a lower-bound condition based on indistinguishable blocks: two laws share the same observed prefix for H rounds but differ in whether a valuable quote crosses after the delay. Use Yao or Le Cam to force regret from actions chosen before the delayed signal arrives.
ideas.title: Minimax Necessity
ideas.why_promising: A defensible only-if theorem must convert meaningful long-tail mass into information-theoretic hardness; this direction isolates the needed quantifiers.

ideas.risks: Naively summing delays over all grid arms may be far too pessimistic; the explorer must exploit full-information and nested-threshold structure.
ideas.summary: Replace fixed-H truncation with arbitrary-delay or skipping delayed-expert algorithms. For grid actions, reveal each reward when its crossing occurs or at horizon, and derive regret in terms of total counted delay, outstanding observations, or weighted skipped payoff. Compare the resulting condition to beta, gamma, and Delta_T.
ideas.title: Skipping Bounds
ideas.why_promising: Modern delayed-learning theory already handles excessive and unbounded delays; translating skip-set bounds may yield a sharper sufficient condition than uniform tail decay.

ideas.risks: Existing one-sided Lipschitz or pricing results often assume immediate or stochastic feedback, so adapting them may not prove the delayed theorem directly.
ideas.summary: Exploit the deterministic identity r_t(a)=a 1{max_{s=t+1..T} P_s > a}; the fixed-action payoff is a times the last crossing time of level a. Investigate adaptive grids, one-sided Lipschitz optimization, and threshold nesting to improve the T/K discretization and identify the real obstruction to no-regret.
ideas.title: Threshold Geometry
ideas.why_promising: The market-making problem is more structured than generic delayed experts: one revealed price resolves an interval of quotes, and comparator payoffs are monotone threshold curves.

ideas.risks: The outcome will depend heavily on the exact meaning of 'possible' and on whether the learner may depend on the process law.
ideas.summary: Systematically test proposed necessary conditions against constructed processes: rare high-value delayed spikes, deterministic predictable sparse spikes, vanishing-value dense spikes, and isolated bad histories. For each, compute beta, gamma, Delta_T, best fixed comparator payoff, and regret of simple learners.
ideas.title: Stress-Test Conditions
ideas.why_promising: This can prevent replacing the false unweighted beta condition with another overly strong condition before a lower-bound theorem is attempted.
